A B S T R A C T
Background
Skin-sparing mastectomy (SSM) is a surgical technique that aims to maximize skin preservation, facilitate breast reconstruction, and
improve cosmetic outcomes. Despite its use in clinical practice, the benefits and harms related to SSM are not well established.
Objectives
To assess the efectiveness and safety of skin-sparing mastectomy for the treatment of breast cancer.
Search methods
We searched Cochrane Breast Cancer's Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, LILACS, the World Health Organization's
International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (WHO ICTRP), and ClinicalTrials.gov on 9 August 2019.
Selection criteria
Randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-randomized or non-randomized studies (cohort and case-control) comparing SSM to
conventional mastectomy for treating ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) or invasive breast cancer.
Data collection and analysis
We used standard methodological procedures expected by Cochrane. The primary outcome was overall survival. Secondary outcomes
were local recurrence free-survival, adverse events (including overall complications, breast reconstruction loss, skin necrosis, infection
and hemorrhage), cosmetic results, and quality of life. We performed a descriptive analysis and meta-analysis of the data.
Main results
We found no RCTs or quasi-RCTs. We included two prospective cohort studies and twelve retrospective cohort studies. These studies
included 12,211 participants involving 12,283 surgeries (3183 SSM and 9100 conventional mastectomies). It was not possible to perform
a meta-analysis for overall survival and local recurrence free-survival due to clinical heterogeneity across studies and a lack of data to
calculate hazard ratios (HR).

Based on one study, the evidence suggests that SSM may not reduce overall survival for participants with DCIS tumors (HR 0.41, 95% CI 0.17
to 1.02; P = 0.06; 399 participants; very low-certainty evidence) or for participants with invasive carcinoma (HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.38; P
= 0.44; 907 participants; very low-certainty evidence). For local recurrence-free survival, meta-analysis was not possible, due to high risk
of bias in nine of the ten studies that measured this outcome. Informal visual examination of efect sizes from nine studies suggested the
size of the HR may be similar between groups. Based on one study that adjusted for confounders, SSM may not reduce local recurrence-
free survival (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.42; P = 0.48; 5690 participants; very low-certainty evidence).
The efect of SSM on overall complications is unclear (RR 1.55, 95% CI 0.97 to 2.46; P = 0.07, I2 = 88%; 4 studies, 677 participants; very
low-certainty evidence). Skin-sparing mastectomy may not reduce the risk of breast reconstruction loss (RR 1.79, 95% CI 0.31 to 10.35; P
= 0.52; 3 studies, 475 participants; very low-certainty evidence), skin necrosis (RR 1.15, 95% CI 0.62 to 2.12; P = 0.22, I2 = 33%; 4 studies,
677 participants; very low-certainty evidence), local infection (RR 2.04, 95% CI 0.03 to 142.71; P = 0.74, I2 = 88%; 2 studies, 371 participants;
very low-certainty evidence), nor hemorrhage (RR 1.23, 95% CI 0.47 to 3.27; P = 0.67, I2 = 0%; 4 studies, 677 participants; very low-certainty
evidence). We downgraded the certainty of the evidence due to the risk of bias, imprecision, and inconsistency among the studies. There
were no data available on the following outcomes: systemic surgical complications, local complications, explantation of implant/expander,
hematoma, seroma, rehospitalization, skin necrosis with revisional surgery, and capsular contracture of the implant.
It was not possible to perform a meta-analysis for cosmetic and quality of life outcomes due to a lack of data. One study performed an
evaluation of aesthetic outcome afer SSM: 77.7% of participants with immediate breast reconstruction had an overall aesthetic result of
excellent or good versus 87% of participants with delayed breast reconstruction.
Authors' conclusions
Based on very low-certainty evidence from observational studies, it was not possible to draw definitive conclusions on the efectiveness
and safety of SSM for breast cancer treatment. The decision for this technique of breast surgery for treatment of DCIS or invasive breast
cancer must be individualized and shared between the physician and the patient while considering the potential risks and benefits of
available surgical options.
P L A I N   L A N G U A G E   S U M M A R Y
Is skin-sparing mastectomy an efective and safe surgical procedure for the treatment of breast cancer?
What is the aim of this review?
We reviewed the evidence about the surgery technique called skin-sparing mastectomy (SSM) (that is, removing the breast tissue including
the breast and areola (skin surrounding the nipple) but preserving all the skin that overlies the breast) compared to conventional
mastectomy (that is, removing the skin that overlies the breast including nipple and areola).
Key messages
We found that SSM may not be diferent from conventional mastectomy for the risk of cancer recurring in the breast area only (local
recurrence), chance of dying of breast cancer (overall survival) or risk of complications afer surgery. Complications afer surgery which
were assessed included breast reconstruction loss (where the breast reconstruction flap or implant needs to be surgically removed due
to complications), skin necrosis, local infection, hemorrhage (bleeding), quality of life, and cosmetic results. The results of this review are
based on 14 studies and most of these with likely biased due to flaws in their design.
What is skin-sparing mastectomy?
Conventional mastectomy for breast cancer is a surgical procedure consisting of removing the entire breast tissue, the skin that overlies
the breast, and the nipple-areola complex. The chance of cancer returning to the chest wall (site of mastectomy) afer this type of
surgery is about 2.3% afer 20 years. Trying to improve cosmetic results has led to the use of skin-sparing mastectomy (SSM) as an
alternative to conventional mastectomy. Preserving as much of the breast skin as possible leaves minimal breast tissue and provides higher
psychological satisfaction and the perception of less injury. SSM has been used for the treatment of breast cancer for the last two decades.
What did we want to find out?
We wanted to find out if SSM is as efective to treat breast cancer as conventional mastectomy and assess whether the surgical complication
rates difered.
What did we do?
We searched for studies that compared SSM with other types of mastectomies for the treatment of breast cancer. We compared and
summarized the results of the studies and rated our confidence in the evidence based on factors such as study methods and sizes.

We found 14 cohort studies (longitudinal studies that follow people over time) involving 12,283 surgeries where 3183 people underwent
an SSM and 9100 underwent a conventional mastectomy. 
People who had an SSM or conventional mastectomy may have similar:
- chance of cancer returning afer surgery (1 study)
- survival (2 studies)
- risk of overall complications (4 studies)
- risk of removing the breast reconstruction flap or implant due to complications (3 studies)
- risk of skin necrosis (4 studies)
- risk of infection (2 studies)
- risk of hemorrhage (4 studies)
However, the evidence is very unclear.
Based on one study, there did not appear to be a diference in aesthetic outcomes between SSM with immediate breast reconstruction
compared to conventional mastectomy and delayed breast reconstruction. One study evaluated the quality of life. The study suggested
similar patient satisfaction, social activity, physical aspects, and general condition in people who have an SSM followed by breast
reconstruction and those who have a mastectomy without breast reconstruction.
What are the limitations of the evidence?
The studies found were mostly retrospective. This means that participants were chosen years afer their surgery, and asked about their
experiences afer surgery, which may have brought bias into the research studies. Of the 14 studies, two studies commenced at the time
of surgery.
People who had conventional mastectomy were likely diferent to those who had SSM. Most studies did not consider these diferences
across groups when analyzing the data.
How up to date is this evidence?
The review authors searched for studies that had been published up to August 2019.

B A C K G R O U N D
Description of the condition
Breast cancer is the most frequent non-skin cancer in women
(24.2% of all cancers in women), with an estimated 2.08 million new
cases and more than 626,679 deaths reported worldwide in 2018
(GLOBOCAN 2018).
Description of the intervention
Skin-sparing mastectomy (SSM) was first described by Toth
1991, in an efort to maximize skin preservation, remove the
nipple-areola complex, improve cosmetic outcome, and facilitate
breast reconstruction. In theory, this technique removes an
equivalent amount of breast tissue and nipple-areola complex
as in conventional mastectomy described by Madden 1965, but
preserves all the skin envelope.
How the intervention might work
SSM greatly enhances the aesthetic results of immediate breast
reconstruction by preserving the skin envelope and the natural
inframammary fold (Carlson 1996; Cunnick 2004; Patani 2008;
Singletary 2003). When SSM is undertaken with immediate breast
reconstruction, it is possible to minimize costs and the need for
further surgeries, to reach a good aesthetic result (Gerber 2009).
Why it is important to do this review
The surgical management of breast carcinoma has evolved during
the past two decades. The improvement in techniques has meant
that more conservative surgery and better cosmetic procedures
can be achieved without compromising oncological safety (Morrow
2002). Surgical strategies have changed significantly, and the
objective of modern breast cancer surgery is to maintain
oncological eficacy and reduce the number of radical procedures
with the goal of minimizing the patient's physical and psychological
trauma (Al-Ghazal 2000). The conservative approach and selective
lymphadenectomy according to sentinel lymph node biopsy, are
examples of this progressive evolution (Cody 2001; Giuliano 1997;
Lyman 2005; Veronesi 1990).
Despite improved early detection and evidence related to the
eficacy of breast-conserving treatment, in some situations, more
radical procedures are still indicated. Conventional surgical therapy
in these situations is radical modified mastectomy (Madden 1965).
Recently, less radical mastectomies, such as SSM and nipple-
sparing mastectomy (NSM), have been proposed as substitutes for
conventional mastectomy in selected patients for the treatment of
breast cancer. Nipple-sparing mastectomy is the focus of another
Cochrane Review (Mota 2016).
Reports have characterized the histological characteristics of
skin flap specimens following SSM. This includes identifying
residual breast tissue or positive superficial margins, which carry
concern for oncological safety and equivalence in maintaining
local control. Torresan and colleagues analyzed the amount of
residual breast tissue afer SSM by histologically analyzing skin
flap specimens and found that 59.5% of specimens contained
residual breast tissue, and 9.5% of skin flaps sheltered residual
disease (Torresan 2005a; Torresan 2005b). In addition, when skin
flaps were greater than 5 mm, they were associated with the
presence of residual disease (Giannotti 2018; Torresan 2005a;
Torresan 2005b). Horiguchi 2006 defined close margins as being
within 5 mm and did find margin status significant on multivariate
analysis of age, hormone receptor-positive lymph node metastasis,
and clinical stage. Medina-Franco 2002 examined the incidence of
local recurrence and factors associated with it in a population of
participants who underwent SSM and immediate reconstruction
for invasive carcinoma. Under univariate analysis, the factors
associated with higher local recurrence rate were tumor stage II or
III, tumor size larger than 2 cm, node-positive disease, and poor
tumor diferentiation. Actuarial one-, three-, and five-year overall
survival rates were 98%, 94%, and 88%, respectively, but under
multivariate analysis, factors associated with decreased survival
were advanced stage and the absence of hormone therapy (Medina-
Franco 2002).
Despite these findings, numerous studies have determined that
SSM is an oncologically safe procedure with no significant
diference in local recurrence compared with conventional
mastectomy. The incidence of local recurrence in data derived
from non-randomized studies ranges from 0% to 7% (Carlson 2003;
Carlson 2007; Gerber 2009; Kroll 1999; Langstein 2003; Medina-
Franco 2002; Newman 1998; Slavin 1998; Spiegel 2003). These
studies include both prospective and retrospective designs and are
dificult to compare, as they vary largely in participant sample size,
stage of disease, tumor characteristics, adjuvant chemotherapy
or radiation therapy, use and type of immediate or delayed
reconstruction, and follow-up time (Tokin 2012). In 2010, a meta-
analysis of observational studies until 2009 concluded that SSM
is an oncologically safe procedure (Lannitis 2010). No significant
diference in local recurrence was noted between SSM versus
non–SSM groups (odds ratio (OR) 1.25, 95% confidence interval
(CI) 0.81 to 1.94; 7 studies, 3436 participants) and no significant
heterogeneity was noted between the studies. The SSM group had
a lower proportion of distant relapses compared with the non–SSM
group (OR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.94; 5 studies, 2122 participants),
but this diference should be interpreted with caution because the
grade of the tumors was not adequately reported in the studies
included in the review (Lannitis 2010).
Despite these data, a new systematic review is necessary to provide
up-to-date evidence concerning the eficacy of SSM and to evaluate
its oncological safety and the quality of life in people who have had
this type of surgery.
O B J E C T I V E S
To assess the efectiveness and safety of skin-sparing mastectomy
(SSM) for the treatment of breast cancer.
M E T H O D S
Criteria for considering studies for this review
Types of studies
We searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs), as they
provide the highest level of evidence. If we found no RCTs eligible
for inclusion in this review, we planned to expand our criteria
to include non-randomized comparative studies. Non-randomized
studies refer to parallel-group studies that closely mirror the
structure of a randomized trial, but with allocation determined
by a non-randomized or quasi-randomized process (e.g. allocation
by patient ID), non-randomized trials, cohort, and case-control
studies.

Non-randomized studies are defined as follows.
•
Prospective cohort study: groups of exposed and nonexposed
individuals that have been followed over time to compare
incidence (or rate of death from disease) between groups (Gordis
1996). In prospective cohort studies, recruitment, exposure or
intervention, and outcomes must all have occurred afer the
study was set up.
•
Retrospective cohort study: groups of exposed and nonexposed
individuals that have been followed over time to compare
incidence (or rate of death from disease) between groups (Gordis
1996). In retrospective cohort studies, outcomes must have
occurred before the study was set up or must have been
collected aferward, or both.
•
Case-control study: a study that compares people with a specific
outcome of interest (cases) versus people from the same source
population but without that outcome (controls), to examine the
association between outcome and prior exposure.
Types of participants
People with a diagnosis of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) or
invasive breast cancer according to the histopathological criteria of
the World Health Organization (Tavassoli 2003), regardless of age,
time of onset, or disease stage.
Types of interventions
Skin-sparing mastectomy (SSM) (i.e. removal of all breast tissue
and the nipple-areola complex and preservation of the entire skin)
compared with conventional mastectomy (i.e. removal of the skin
that overlies the breast including the nipple and areola, as well as
removal of all breast tissue) for the treatment of DCIS or invasive
breast cancer, regardless of adjuvant therapy.
In this review, the SSM arm included people who have had any kind
of breast reconstructive surgery, and the conventional mastectomy
arm included people who had or did not have breast reconstructive
surgery.
Types of outcome measures
Primary outcomes
•
Overall survival: time to death during the follow-up period,
considered separately for ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) and
early breast cancer
Secondary outcomes
•
Local recurrence-free survival: time-to-event for recurrence
during the follow-up period, and considered separately for DCIS
and early breast cancer
•
Breast cancer-specific survival: time from either the date of
diagnosis or the start of treatment for breast cancer to the date
of death from the disease
•
Adverse events: local or systemic surgical complications, such as
thromboembolic events, up until three months afer surgery
◦ Overall complications
◦ Hemorrhage
◦ Breast reconstruction loss
◦ Local Complications
◦ Explantation of implant/expander
◦ Hematoma
◦ Seroma
◦ Rehospitalization
◦ Skin necrosis (nipple, areola, or flap necrosis)
◦ Skin necrosis with revisional surgery
◦ Capsular contracture of the implant
◦ Infection
•
Cosmetic results: using the BREAST-Q questionnaire (Pusic
2009). When no validated instrument was included in
the studies, participant and professional opinions were
documented.
•
Quality of life and participant satisfaction: using the EORTC QLQ-
BR23 (Fayers 1999) and BREAST-Q (Pusic 2009) questionnaires.
When no validated instrument was included in the studies,
participant and professional opinions were documented.
Search methods for identification of studies
Electronic searches
We searched the following databases.
•
The Cochrane Breast Cancer's Specialized Register. Details of
the search strategies used by the Group for the identification of
studies and the procedure used to code references are outlined
on the Group's website. Trials with the keywords "breast cancer,"
"skin-sparing mastectomy," "segmental mastectomy," "breast
conserving surgery," "partial mastectomy," and "lumpectomy"
were extracted and considered for inclusion in the review.
•
Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL; 2019;
Issue 7) in The Cochrane Library (see Appendix 1).
•
MEDLINE Ovid (1946 to 9 August 2019; see Appendix 2).
•
EMBASE Ovid (1947 to 9 August 2019; see Appendix 3).
•
LILACS (Latin American and Caribbean Health Science
Information database; 1982 to 9 August 2019; see Appendix 4).
•
World Health Organization's International Clinical Trials Registry
Platform (apps.who.int/trialsearch; searched 9 August 2019; see
Appendix 5).
•
US National Institutes of Health Ongoing Trials Register
ClinicalTrials.gov (www.clinicaltrials.gov; searched 9 August
2019; see Appendix 6).
Searching other resources
We searched the bibliographies of all included studies and review
papers, in order to identify other potentially eligible studies. Where
possible, we obtained a copy of the full article for each reference
reporting a potentially eligible trial. We contacted study authors
to provide additional information when it was not available. We
applied no language restrictions.
Data collection and analysis
Selection of studies
We downloaded all titles and abstracts retrieved by electronic
searching to a reference management database and removed
duplicates. Two review authors (BSM and MDR) independently
screened titles and abstracts for inclusion. We retrieved the full-
text reports and two review authors independently applied the
eligibility criteria to the full texts, identified studies for inclusion,
and identified and recorded reasons for exclusion of ineligible
studies. We resolved any disagreement through discussion or,

We recorded the selection process in suficient detail to complete a

Data extraction and management
We developed data extraction forms and two review authors (BSM
and MDR) independently extracted data and consulted a third
author (JLBB) to help resolve disagreements. Where necessary,
we sought unpublished data concerning outcomes of interest by
contacting study authors.
We included the following information from individual studies in
the data extraction forms:
•
publication details;
•
study design, study setting, inclusion and exclusion criteria;
•
patient population e.g. age, type of surgical procedure,
histological classification;
•
details of intervention;
•
outcome measures; and
•
withdrawals, length and method of follow-up, and the number
of participants followed up.
For non-randomized studies, we also recorded the following
information:
•
methods used to control for confounders; and
•
adjusted and unadjusted outcome measures.
We entered quantitative data into RevMan Web 2020 sofware to
carry out the analyses.
Assessment of risk of bias in included studies
We followed Cochrane’s tool for assessing risk of bias, as
described in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews
of Interventions (Higgins 2011), Cochrane EPOC 2013 risk of
bias criteria, and recommendations by Norris 2013. Assessment

Measures of treatment efect
We reported treatment efect measures for time-to-event outcomes
(e.g. overall survival, local recurrence free-survival) as hazard ratios
(HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). When only published
survival curves were available, we calculated HRs using the Parmar
1998  method, which assumes that censoring occurs uniformly
between the minimum and maximum follow-up times reported in
the study. In the absence of individual patient data, it is possible
to derive HRs and/or associated statistics by the of published or
other summary using the method of Williamson (Williamson 2002),
or spreadsheet published by Tierney 2007 to estimate the HRs.
We reported treatment efect measures for dichotomous outcomes
(i.e. overall complications, breast reconstruction loss, explantation
of implant/expander, hematoma, seroma, rehospitalization, skin
necrosis (nipple, areola, or flap necrosis), revisional surgery,
infection, and cosmetic results) as risk ratios (RR). We pooled the
data for meta-analysis using the pooled log RR, when appropriate.
We reported treatment efect measures for continuous outcomes
(e.g. quality of life) as standardized mean diferences (SMD) with
95% CIs.
Where possible, we extracted efect estimates adjusted for our
pre-specified list of possible confounders (adjuvant treatment as
chemotherapy and radiotherapy, age, surgical techniques, stage
of disease, DCIS, or invasive breast cancer). If studies provided
adjusted efect estimates but did not adjust for all confounders
named in our pre-specified list, we recorded the confounders for
which studies had adjusted.
As conventional mastectomy is the standard treatment for DCIS or
invasive breast cancer, it seems reasonable to consider skin-sparing
mastectomy as a non-inferiority question. Thus, the non-inferiority
bound HR for overall survival was 1.13 (based on a 10-year survival
rate of 27% for conventional mastectomy with a cutof value of
24% for SSM). For local recurrence, the non-inferiority bound HR
was 2.67 (based on 3% 10-year local recurrence for conventional
mastectomy with a cutof value of 8% for SSM).
Unit of analysis issues
The unit of analysis was the individual participant, rather than the
breast, surgical unit, hospital, or center.
Dealing with missing data
When data were missing or unsuitable for analysis (e.g. intention-
to-treat data were not used), we contacted the study authors to
request further information.
When data were missing to the extent that the study could not
be included in the meta-analysis and attempts to retrieve data
had been exhausted, we presented the results in the review and
discussed the context of the findings.
Assessment of heterogeneity
If appropriate, we assessed the presence of statistical
heterogeneity using the Chi2 statistic (Cochran 1954). We
investigated its extent by the use of the I2 statistic, which
estimates the percentage of total variation across studies due to
heterogeneity rather than chance. An I2 value of 30% to 60% may
represent moderate heterogeneity, and values greater than 50%
may be considered to show substantial heterogeneity (Higgins
2003).
We investigated the following factors as potential causes of
heterogeneity in the included studies using the framework below.
•
Clinical diversity: included study location and setting, full
characteristics of participants, comorbidities, and treatments
that participants were probably receiving on study entry. We
considered how outcomes were measured, the definition of
outcomes, and how they were recorded. Depending upon the
extent of the clinical diversity, we analyzed studies either
separately or presented the results using a narrative approach.
•

Where meta-analyses were not possible, we used the Synthesis
Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) approach (McKenzie 2021), and
assessed heterogeneity by visually inspecting forest plots.
Assessment of reporting biases
We searched for protocols of included trials using PubMed
(National Library of Medicine) and other trial registries, when
possible. We contacted study authors in an attempt to acquire a
full data set or establish reasons for the non-reporting of certain
outcomes. When 10 or more studies were available for a meta-
analysis, we intended to develop a funnel plot to investigate
publication bias.
Data synthesis
If we included randomized and non-randomized studies, we
intended to synthesize their data separately.
We planned to synthesize data using a random-efects model
by default, since we expected clinical or methodological
heterogeneity, or both, among studies (DerSimonian 1986). Where
possible, we combined data using the inverse variance method on
the log HR scale for time-to-event outcomes, and on the log RR
scale for dichotomous outcomes.

we anticipated that a substantial number of the reported study
results may be subject to bias due to inadequate adjustment for
confounding. In the case of high or unclear risk of selection bias due

Subgroup analysis and investigation of heterogeneity
As we expected a small number of published studies, we did not
envisage that it would be possible to perform subgroup analyses.
However, in review updates, we would like to consider the following
subgroups when assessing the primary outcomes.
•
Participants who received adjuvant radiotherapy versus
participants who did not receive radiotherapy.
•
Age: younger (< 50 years of age) versus older (≥ 50 years of age)
participants.
•
Cancer stage as per TNM (size and/or extent of the primary tumor
[T], amount of spread to nearby lymph nodes [N], and presence
of metastasis [M] or secondary tumors) classification system
(Brierley 2017).
•
Systemic therapy (chemotherapy or endocrine therapy) versus
no systemic therapy.
•
Molecular subtype.
We based these planned subgroups on published evidence that the
intervention efect could be modified by these characteristics.
Sensitivity analysis
We planned to conduct sensitivity analyses by excluding either
studies of low methodological quality or, if RCT evidence was
available, quasi-randomized studies. This was not possible due
to a lack of high-quality studies, but we will consider sensitivity
analyses for future updates of this review.
Summary of findings and assessment of the certainty of the
evidence
We created a summary of findings table for the main outcomes
for the comparison of SSM versus conventional mastectomy. Three
review authors (BSM, MDR and RR) independently assessed the
certainty of the evidence using the GRADE framework. We used
the five GRADE criteria (study limitations, consistency of efect,
imprecision, indirectness, and publication bias) to assess the
certainty of the evidence, and we reported this certainty as either
high, moderate, low, or very low. We considered the following
criteria for upgrading the certainty of evidence, if appropriate:
large efect and dose-response gradient. We used the methods and
recommendations described in Section 8.5 and 8.7, and Chapters
11 and 12, of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews
of Interventions (Higgins 2011; Schünemann 2011a; Schünemann
2011b). Where we adopted a SWiM approach, we did not report
absolute and relative efects, but we did assess the certainty of the
evidence using the GRADE framework.
We used GRADEpro GDT to prepare the summary of findings
tables. We justified all decisions to downgrade or upgrade the
certainty of the evidence using footnotes and made comments
to aid the reader's understanding of the review where necessary.
We selected the following outcomes for the summary of findings
tables: overall survival, local recurrence-free survival, overall
complications, breast reconstruction loss, skin necrosis, infection,
and hemorrhage.
To calculate the absolute risk for the control group for time-to-
event outcomes, we estimated the event rate at a specific time
point (i.e. five-year time point for both overall survival for invasive
breast cancer and local recurrence-free survival; 10-year time point
for overall survival for DCIS) from the Kaplan-Meier curves or based
upon an average of the estimates from studies.

Included studies

Study design
We did not find any randomized or quasi-randomized trials. All
included studies were cohorts. Two were prospective cohorts
(Gerber 2009; Simmons 1999). The remaining 12 studies were
retrospective cohorts (Carlson 1997; Giacalone 2010; Greenway
2005; Kinoshita 2011; Kroll 1999; Lee 2018; Lhenaf 2019; Lim 2010;
Min 2011; Prabhu 2011; Timbrell 2017; Ueda 2008).
Characteristics of participants
Sample size
The studies included 12,211 participants involving 12,283 surgeries:
3183 underwent skin-sparing mastectomy (SSM), and 9100
underwent conventional mastectomy.
Age of participants
In terms of age see Table 1, five studies did not describe if there
were any diferences in terms of age between groups (Carlson 1997;
Greenway 2005; Kroll 1999; Lee 2018; Lhenaf 2019). Nine studies
found that the SSM group was younger than the conventional
mastectomy group (Gerber 2009; Giacalone 2010; Kinoshita 2011;
Lim 2010; Min 2011; Prabhu 2011; Simmons 1999; Timbrell 2017;
Ueda 2008).
Reason for breast surgery
The majority of participants had a mastectomy due to invasive
breast carcinoma (83.3%), followed by ductal carcinoma in situ
(DCIS) or preventative reasons (i.e. for women with a high risk of
breast cancer) (15.4%). The reason was not described for some
participants (1.3%).
Disease stage
Two studies included participants with stage 0 breast cancer
(Lhenaf 2019; Timbrell 2017); seven studies included participants
with stage 0, I, II, and III (Gerber 2009; Greenway 2005; Kinoshita
2011; Lee 2018; Min 2011; Simmons 1999; Ueda 2008); two studies
included participants with stage II or III (Giacalone 2010; Lim 2010);
one study included only participants with stage III (Prabhu 2011);
one included people with all stages (0 to IV) and for prophylactic
reasons (Carlson 1997); and one study did not mention tumor stage
but included participants with T1 or T2 tumors (Kroll 1999).
Intervention and comparators
•
SSM versus conventional mastectomy: 12 studies (Carlson 1997;
Giacalone 2010; Greenway 2005; Kinoshita 2011; Kroll 1999; Lee
2018; Lhenaf 2019; Lim 2010; Min 2011; Prabhu 2011; Simmons
1999; Timbrell 2017);
•
SSM 
versus

(NSM) 
versus
conventional mastectomy: one study (Gerber 2009);
•
SSM versus conventional mastectomy versus conservative
surgery: one study (Ueda 2008).
In four studies, a few cases of NSM were included in the SSM arm
(Lee 2018; Lim 2010; Min 2011; Ueda 2008).
Adjuvant therapy
Thirteen studies described the adjuvant therapy treatment
(chemotherapy or radiotherapy) (Gerber 2009; Giacalone 2010;
Greenway 2005; Kinoshita 2011; Kroll 1999; Lee 2018; Lhenaf 2019;
Lim 2010; Min 2011; Prabhu 2011; Simmons 1999; Timbrell 2017;
Ueda 2008). One study did not provide any information on adjuvant
therapy (Carlson 1997).
In the two studies on more advanced disease, all participants
received adjuvant therapy (chemotherapy and radiotherapy)
(Giacalone 2010; Prabhu 2011). In all other studies, the indication
of adjuvant therapy was based on clinical practice guidelines, and
these studies did not report the percentage of participants who
received adjuvant therapy or details of the type of adjuvant therapy.
Follow-up
Five studies had a mean follow-up of 60 months or longer (Gerber
2009; Lee 2018; Lhenaf 2019; Lim 2010; Timbrell 2017). Six studies
had a mean follow-up of 40 to 60 months (Carlson 1997; Giacalone
2010; Greenway 2005; Kroll 1999; Min 2011; Ueda 2008). Three
studies had a mean follow-up of fewer than 40 months (Kinoshita
2011; Prabhu 2011; Simmons 1999).
Two studies used methods to adjust for diferential follow-up
between the intervention and comparator groups. Kinoshita 2011
reported a mean follow-up of 30.0 months (standard deviation
(SD) 22.6) in the SSM group versus 41.1 months (SD 21.3) in the
conventional mastectomy group (P < 0.000, as reported in the
publication). Simmons 1999 had a median follow-up time of 15.6
months (range 2.7 to 96.0 months) in the SSM group versus 32.4
months (range 1.0 to 98.4 months) in the conventional mastectomy
group (P < 0.001).
Excluded studies
We excluded Park 2016 because data were not presented separately
for the SSM group in the study group. It was a retrospective
cohort study comparing participants who underwent any kind of
mastectomy (SSM and total mastectomy) plus immediate breast
reconstruction versus participants who underwent mastectomy
alone. We contacted the study author, but it was not possible to
reorganize the data.

Allocation
The most common source of potential bias was selection bias.
All studies were cohort studies: two were prospective (Gerber
2009; Simmons 1999), and 12 were retrospective (Carlson 1997;
Giacalone 2010; Greenway 2005; Kinoshita 2011; Kroll 1999; Lee
2018; Lhenaf 2019; Lim 2010; Min 2011; Prabhu 2011; Timbrell
2017; Ueda 2008). None of the studies had an allocation sequence
adequately generated and concealed, and we judged all to be at
high risk of selection bias.
Eight studies reported an age diference between groups with
younger participants in the SSM group than the conventional
mastectomy group (Gerber 2009; Giacalone 2010; Kinoshita 2011;
Lim 2010; Min 2011; Simmons 1999; Timbrell 2017; Ueda 2008).
Two studies included a higher proportion of people with early-
stage tumors in the SSM compared to conventional mastectomy
group (Lee 2018; Min 2011). Two studies had shorter follow-up
in the SSM group than in the conventional mastectomy group
(Kinoshita 2011; Simmons 1999). Four studies had diferences in
adjuvant treatment, whereby radiotherapy, chemotherapy, or both
were performed more frequently in the SSM than conventional
mastectomy group (Gerber 2009; Giacalone 2010; Lee 2018; Min
2011). Overall, we assessed these above-mentioned studies as
having a high risk of bias for baseline characteristics. One study
reported similar baseline characteristics between mastectomy
groups; we judged it as having a low risk of bias (Prabhu 2011).
One study performed 1:1 propensity score matching to overcome
selection bias but only for the outcome of breast cancer-specific
survival (Lee 2018). We judged it as having a low risk of bias
for confounders. None of the other studies used appropriate
techniques to deal with the potential confounders pre-specified
for this review. The remaining studies made no adjustment
for confounding, and we assessed them as having a high risk
of selection bias (Carlson 1997; Gerber 2009; Giacalone 2010;
Greenway 2005; Kinoshita 2011; Kroll 1999; Lhenaf 2019; Lim 2010;
Min 2011; Prabhu 2011; Simmons 1999; Timbrell 2017; Ueda 2008).

Blinding of participants and surgeons was not possible due to the

Overall survival and local recurrence-free survival were considered
objective outcomes; consequently, a lack of blinding was unlikely

2019; Lim 2010). We judged the remaining studies to have a high
probability of detection bias because it was not stated if the local
recurrence was histologically confirmed.
The lack of blinding may have influenced the results for subjective

concerning social activity (six items), physical aspects (five items),

D I S C U S S I O N
Summary of main results
This review included 14 comparative observational studies (two
prospective and 12 retrospective cohort studies) comparing
the efects of skin-sparing mastectomy (SSM) and conventional
mastectomy as surgical options for people with ductal carcinoma
in situ (DCIS) or invasive breast cancer. Based on very few studies,
the efect of SSM may be similar to conventional mastectomy for
the following outcomes:
•
overall survival (very low-certainty evidence);
•
local recurrence free-survival (low-certainty evidence);
•
overall complications (very low-certainty evidence);
•
breast reconstruction loss (very low-certainty evidence);
•
skin necrosis and infection (very low-certainty evidence);
•
hemorrhage (very low certainty-evidence).
In addition, the findings are subject to a high risk of selection bias
as 13 out of 14 included studies did not adequately adjust for
confounding.
Overall completeness and applicability of evidence
The overall completeness of evidence is limited by a lack of data
for the outcomes of interest due to the low number of studies,
small study population sizes, and few observed events. In addition,
clinical heterogeneity among studies meant we could not conduct
the meta-analyses that could help overcome these limitations.
There is a lack of evidence for all outcomes: additional studies are
likely to have an important impact on the estimated efect of the
interventions compared.
Given that this review included only observational studies, we
expect that the study populations and interventions considered
are very consistent with those observed in clinical practice. This
wide scope improves the external validity of the review and the
applicability of the findings.
Certainty of the evidence
We present our assessments of the certainty of evidence obtained
for each outcome in Summary of findings 1. We downgraded the
overall certainty of the evidence at study or outcome levels due
to the poor methodological quality of included studies. All studies
were cohort studies with no allocation sequence generation,
allocation concealment, or blinding of participants, personnel,
or outcome assessors. Furthermore, results were imprecise and
inconsistent (due to wide CIs and small samples). The risk of bias
due to confounding was very high because adequate adjustment
for confounding was not carried out by 13 out of 14 studies included
in this review.
For overall survival, local recurrence free-survival, and breast
cancer-specific survival, the CIs for efect estimates were very
wide. Results for DCIS and invasive tumors indicate that SSM is
consistent with both benefit and harm. This imprecision is due to
a low number of events and clinical heterogeneity among included
studies. Due to the very low-certainty evidence in our review, we
cannot make any conclusions for practice.
For complication rates, we downgraded the certainty of the
evidence due to methodological limitations, inconsistency,
imprecision (CI including null efect), and confounding factors.
Potential biases in the review process
The main limitations of this systematic review are due to
the methodological deficiencies of the included studies. The
evidence in this review came from observational studies (mostly
retrospective and of low methodological quality), which are subject
to important biases that increase the uncertainty of the results.
It was not possible to calculate HRs for the assessment of survival
data for all studies because many studies did not report time-to-
event analyses in suficient detail. Due to these reasons, it was not
possible to perform subgroup analysis, and analyses for overall
survival, aesthetic and quality of life outcomes as initially proposed
in the published protocol.
There were potential biases in the review process. Carrying out
reviews requires a number of subjective judgements, and it is
possible that a diferent review team may have reached diferent
decisions regarding the assessments of eligibility and risks of
bias. Feedback from readers will serve to improve the next review
update. Although the review authors’ views varied, we decided to
accept the final conclusions afer extensive discussion to reach a
consensus.

Agreements and disagreements with other studies or
reviews
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic review
of observational studies on this topic to evaluate the certainty of
evidence through an appropriate tool (GRADE). There are some
similar systematic reviews but only one, Lannitis 2010, showed
similar results between patients who had undergone conventional
mastectomy and SSM. Lannitis 2010 included nine studies and
the authors found no diference between SSM and conventional
mastectomy.
The most important methodological diferences between Lannitis
2010 and our review are:
•
Lannitis 2010 used the OR to estimate the efects of time-to-
event outcomes. We performed these analyses using HRs (which
is considered more appropriate);
•
Lannitis 2010 assessed only the methodological quality and risk
of bias of the included studies and did not assess the overall
certainty of the evidence for each outcome.
A U T H O R S '   C O N C L U S I O N S
Implications for practice
Surgeons are increasingly performing skin-sparing mastectomy
(SSM) and related surgeries (such as nipple-sparing mastectomy)
for treating breast cancer. In most breast cancer centers in the
world, SSM now seems to be the standard surgical treatment when
conservative surgery (lumpectomy) is not an option. This review
showed the absence of randomized clinical trials to evaluate the
eficacy and safety of SSM in breast cancer treatment. The evidence
found by this review suggests that SSM could be a safe approach,
but this finding is limited mainly due to a lack of randomized clinical
trials and poor reporting from observational studies. Additional
research is therefore likely to have an important impact on the
estimated efect.
The decision to perform this breast surgery for treatment should be
individualized and shared between the physician and the patient,
considering the potential risks and benefits of each intervention.
Implications for research
Randomized controlled clinical trials (RCTs) are considered the gold
standard for evidence-based medicine and are crucial for guiding
medical practice through consistent scientific observations. The
main advantage of clinical trials is that randomization reduces the
chance of selection bias and a confounding efect. Randomization
may not be feasible in this surgical field due to the nature of
the intervention, and it could substantially increase the cost
of performing the research. Consequently, addressing this issue
necessitates a balance between practicability and methodological
rigor; in particular, a rigorous design to eliminate flaws that could
render the results invalid.
This review showed the absence of randomized clinical trials to
evaluate the efectiveness and safety of SSM in people diagnosed
with ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) or invasive breast cancer.
We suggest that future RCTs should:
•
use the CONSORT Statement (CONSORT) to guide study method;
•
use standardized criteria to define outcomes and report the time
at which the outcome is measured; and
•
include long-term follow-up.
When an RCT is not feasible, we suggest cohort studies should:
•
use STROBE guidelines (von Elm 2007);
•
use standardized criteria to define outcomes and report the time
at which the outcome is measured;
•
include long-term follow-up;
•
use appropriate adjustment for follow-up time in the analysis of
outcomes by using survival analysis methods or person-years of
follow-up as the denominator for the incidence rates for events
of interest; and
•
use propensity score matching - a statistical technique that
attempts to estimate the efect of a treatment by accounting for
the covariates that predict receiving the treatment.

Outcomes
•
We changed 'local recurrence' to 'local recurrence-free survival' for a better comparison when describing the absolute risk outcome.
•
We added 'breast cancer-specific survival' as a secondary outcome, as multiple studies reported this outcome.
Analyses
•
Due to a lack of data, we could not perform subgroup analysis and comparisons of some of the adverse events - local or systemic
surgical complications - as proposed in the protocol. We included the analysis of overall complications, breast reconstruction loss, and
hemorrhage, as these outcomes were reported in most studies. 'Overall complications' included systemic surgical complications and
local complications together.
•
Due to a lack of data, we could not perform meta-analysis for cosmetic results and quality of life.
